Q: Compiler complaining about non-copy-assingnable type despite a condition ensuring it is A:

You're getting the error because of a combination of two factors:

  1. Your type is apparently not trivially-copy-assignable (unfortunate, as std::optional is trivially-copy-assignable I believe).
  2. Your condition is a run-time condition, i.e. the compiler is not guaranteed to completely ignore the "then" branch, as it would with C++17's if constexpr.

Still, GCC (16.2) could have noticed that you'll never actually perform the copy for an inappropriate type, and spared you that warning. clang 23.1 does so. You could perhaps file a bug report about this.

Q: Linux mount fails with error Transport endpoint not connected A:

I know this is old but it might help others facing this issue. We had a similar problem with our bucket being unmounted randomly and getting the 'Transport endpoint is not connected' error.

Instead of using "cat /etc/mtab", I use "df -hT" and it works with my script. The problem is it gets stuck in this weird state, of being half unmounted and the "mtab" still sees it as mounted; but I still don't know why.

This is the code I'm using:

#!/bin/bash

if [ $(df -hT | grep -c s3fs) != 1 ]
then 
        # unmount it first
        umount /path/to/mounted/bucket;

        # remount it
        /usr/local/bin/s3fs bucket-name /path/to/mount/bucket -o noatime -o allow_other;

        echo "s3fs is down";

        # maybe send email here to let you know it went down
fi

Also make sure you run your script as root, otherwise it won't be able to unmount/remount.

Q: Computer Vision: How do I use a thermal image as an alpha channel with an RBG image with OpenCV and Python? A:

Here are some alternatives in Python, OpenCV and Mathplotlib.

  • Read the 4-channel color image without the 4th channel

  • Read the 4-channel thermal image as grayscale

  • Original method:

    • Split the color image channels

    • Combine b, g, r, thermal to form the first original result

  • Alternate 1 - enhanced method

    • Change all pixels in the thermal image below a threshold to black

    • Stretch the contrast of the thermal

    • Combine b, g, r, thermal to form the first enhanced result

  • Alternate2 - enhance method plotted with gray background

  • Alternate2 - enhance method plotted with black background

  • Plot all 4 results in one plot

  • Save the plot to disk

Color image:

Thermal image:

import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
#import matplotlib.image as mpimg

# read 4 channelimages without 4th channel
# read thermal image as grayscale
bgr_img = cv2.imread("color.png")
th_img = cv2.imread("thermal.png", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

# split channel for color image
b, g, r = cv2.split(bgr_img)

# combine color channels with thermal image
bgrth_img = cv2.merge([b, g, r, th_img])


# Alternate 1 - force background to black and enhance contract
temp = th_img.copy()
temp[temp<30] = 0
th_img2 = cv2.normalize(temp, dst=None, alpha=0, beta=350, norm_type=cv2.NORM_MINMAX, dtype=cv2.CV_8U)
bgrth_img2 = cv2.merge([b, g, r, th_img2])

# Alternate 2 - change background color of plt to gray
# see below

# Alternate 3 - change background color of plt to black 
# see below
Alternate2 - enhance method plotted with gray background

# show  and save result
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10,7))  # figsize in inches
axes[0,0].imshow(bgrth_img)
axes[0,0].set_title('Original Combined')

axes[0,1].imshow(bgrth_img2)
axes[0,1].set_title('Enhanced Combined')

axes[1,0].imshow(bgrth_img2)
axes[1,0].set_title('Enhanced Combined with Gray')
axes[1,0].set_facecolor('#999999')

axes[1,1].imshow(bgrth_img2)
axes[1,1].set_title('Enhanced Combined with Black')
axes[1,1 ].set_facecolor('black')


plt.tight_layout()

# save the figure to disk
plt.savefig('color_thermal_results.png', dpi=72, bbox_inches='tight')

plt.show()

Q: Amazon SES: BadRequestException and HTTP Body: {"message":null} A:

{"message":null} doesn't mean the message body is null, it means there is no specific error message. Were it not to be null, I would have expected something like {"message":"Source must not be null"}

You should look at the response's Reason/Status phrase (which may or may not be returned) and I would expect that to be something like ValidationError according to the documentation.

Q: Is there a way to make scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') accurate? A:

If I understand correctly, method="trust-constr" is considered to be the most modern, highest-quality, and currently-best-supported of the strategies available for scipy.optimize.minimize() when doing constrained minimization.

I would quibble with this. I would say that COBYQA (added in SciPy 1.14) is the most modern and most generally useful minimization method in SciPy. (It is outcompeted on certain problems by SLSQP, but COBYQA is less prone to SLSQP's numerical weirdness.) COBYQA is what I would recommend to most new users who need to optimize a constrained function.

I'm optimizing a nonlinear function with nonlinear constraints, and I'd like a double-precision-ish answer. I've distilled it down to a problem that demonstrates the issue: namely, the cosine function, which is representative of my problem in the relevant regards. Adding more details about my original large application would be distracting and counterproductive, in my judgement, so I'm not going to do that.

It's really hard to give you useful tuning advice without seeing your real problem, or at least a much closer approximation of your problem.

Let me give you an example of why. In your initial code, you set the parameter barrier_tol. This parameter adjusts the termination condition due to trust region size decreasing too much. However, this parameter doesn't do anything for problems without inequality constraints, because barrier_tol only does something if the tr_interior_point sub-method of trust-constr is selected, which only happens if you have inequality constraints.

In order to tell you whether adjusting barrier_tol will help, I need to know if your real problem has inequality constraints.

For comparison, the program also contains a little Newton's-method solver. Given the same information as was given to scipy.optimize.minimize() (the gradient and hessian, asking it to find where the gradient is zero) the Newton solver always converges to exactly the right answer (to machine precision) math.pi, in 7 or fewer iterations, as expected, on each of the initial guesses. I expect 'trust-constr' to be able to do this too.

SciPy contains a lot of code to handle the corner cases in optimization. This is one of the cases where that extra code isn't helping.

trust-constr is a trust region approximation method, which means that it builds an approximation of the problem, then solves the approximation, then uses that for future guesses. The cos() function in this case is really poorly approximated by a quadratic once you get within 1e-8 of the right answer. trust-constr reacts to this by reducing the trust region size, so that it takes smaller and smaller steps. But the problem is that there is no trust-region size small enough to help. The problem is discontinuous around the right answer.

"Some optimisers will find the ends of the range of contiguous zeros and return the mid point but evidently scipi doesn't do this". Hmm, I didn't expect it to search for the ends of the range of zeros, I expected it to simply find the point at which the gradient function is zero (within gtol). But I guess, for these surprisingly early terminations, it's stopping due to xtol (a criterion I don't understand as well) instead, no matter how tiny xtol is chosen to be? I wonder whether this is really intended behavior-- I'd expect the trust-region feature to only improve behavior, not make it worse.

Most termination conditions in SciPy are OR, not AND. The method will stop if the xtol termination condition asks it to stop, OR if gtol asks it to stop. If it terminates due to xtol, it will not search around for a smaller gradient. It will just stop there.

This means that you can in some cases improve precision by reformulating a minimization problem as a root-finding problem. Here is an example of how this can improve precision.

This is applicable to this example too:

#!/usr/bin/python3

import math
import scipy
import warnings

max_newton_iterations_ever = 0
def simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(f, df, initial_guess):  # {
  global max_newton_iterations_ever
  print(f"            in simple_newton_solver_for_comparison")
  x = initial_guess
  for i in range(100):
    max_newton_iterations_ever = max(max_newton_iterations_ever, i+1)
    fx = f(x)
    dfx = df(x)
    newx = x - fx/dfx
    print(f"              i={i}: {x} - {fx}/{dfx} -> {newx}")
    if newx == x:
      print(f"                  (which is the same as previous, so converged)")
      break  # not really reliable for general problems since it could oscillate between two or more values, but whatever
    x = newx
  else:
    # didn't break
    raise AssertionError("oh no, simple_newton_solver_for_comparison didn't converge")
  print(f"            out simple_newton_solver_for_comparison, returning {x}")
  return x
# }

# The test problem: find a local minimum of y=cos(x)
def fun(x):           return math.cos(x[0])
def analytic_jac(x):  return [-math.sin(x[0])]
def analytic_hess(x): return [[-math.cos(x[0])]]
    

table_data = []
for initial_guess in [
  # (smaller than this finds a different min or max)
  2.0,  # resulting error is -2.893161266115385e-10
  2.5,  # 2.013678113144124e-11
  2.75,  # 0.0
  2.931166343,  # 0.0
  2.931166344,  # -1.053671194739536e-08
  3.0,  # -2.893161266115385e-10
  3.1,  # -4.440892098500626e-15
  3.14,  # 1.346614375563604e-09
  3.141,  # 6.938760677144273e-11
  3.1415,  # 2.651212582804874e-13
  3.14159,  # 0.0
  3.141592,  # 0.0
  3.1415926,  # 0.0
  3.14159265,  # -3.589792907376932e-09  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped at initial guess)
  3.141592653,  # -5.892171195398532e-10  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  3.1415926535,  # -8.979306187484326e-11  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  3.14159265358,  # -9.793055255613581e-12  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  3.141592653589,  # -7.931433287922118e-13  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  3.1415926535897,  # -9.325873406851315e-14  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  3.14159265358979,  # -3.1086244689504383e-15  (note these are the remaining digits of pi, so it just stopped)
  math.pi,  # 0.0,  not surprising
  3.5,  # 0.0
  4.0,  # -2.893161266115385e-10
  # (larger than this finds a different min or max)
]:  # {
  print(f"  =========================")
  print(f"  initial_guess = {initial_guess}")
  print(f"      Doing it using scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr')")
  with warnings.catch_warnings():  # local scope for temporarily changing the way warnings are handled
    warnings.simplefilter("error")  # temporarily change warnings into fatal exceptions (errors)
    print(f"          calling scipy.optimize.minimize")
    
    minimize_via_root = scipy.optimize.root(analytic_jac, x0=[initial_guess], method='hybr')
  scipy_answer = float(minimize_via_root.x[0])
  print(f"          scipy_answer = {scipy_answer}")
  scipy_error = scipy_answer - math.pi
  print(f"          scipy_error = abs:{scipy_error} rel:{scipy_error/math.pi}")
  assert minimize_via_root.success

  print(f"      Doing it using simple_newton_solver_for_comparison")
  my_answer = simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(
    f=lambda x:analytic_jac([x])[0],
    df=lambda x:analytic_hess([x])[0][0],
    initial_guess=initial_guess,
  )
  assert analytic_hess([my_answer])[0][0] > 0.0  # make sure it's a minimum, not a maximum or stationary point of inflection
  print(f"          my_answer = {my_answer}")
  my_error = my_answer - math.pi
  print(f"          my_error = abs:{my_error} rel:{my_error/math.pi}")

  table_data.append({
    "initial_guess":initial_guess,
    "scipy_answer":scipy_answer,
    "scipy_error":scipy_error,
    "scipy_error relative":scipy_error/math.pi,
    "my_answer":my_answer,
    "my_error":my_error,
  })

  print(f"  =========================")
# }  for initial_guess


# `data` is a list of dicts mapping column name to numeric value.
# All the dicts must have the same keys (column names).
def FormatTable(data):  # {
  if len(data) == 0:
    return ""
  keys = data[0].keys()
  for datum in data:
    assert datum.keys() == keys  # every row has the same keys
  rows_of_cells = [list(keys)] + [[f"{v!r}" for v in datum.values()] for datum in data]
  colwidths = [max(len(cell) for cell in col) for col in zip(*rows_of_cells, strict=True)]
  def pad_cell(cell, width):
    if 'e-' in cell:
      # hacky condition but it seems right for this program's data at this time:
      # right-justify the numbers that are in exponential notation,
      # left-justifify the other numbers.
      return cell.rjust(width, ' ')
    else:
      return cell.ljust(width, ' ')
  answer_lines = []
  separator_line = "+"+"+".join('-'*colwidth for colwidth in colwidths)+"+"
  for irow,row_of_cells in list(enumerate(rows_of_cells)):
    if irow <= 1:
      answer_lines.append(separator_line)
    answer_lines.append("|"+"|".join(pad_cell(cell,width) for cell,width in zip(row_of_cells,colwidths,strict=True))+"|")
  answer_lines.append(separator_line)
  return '\n'.join(answer_lines)
# }  FormatTable


print(f"==================================================")
print(f"Summary:")
print(FormatTable(table_data));
scipy_max_abs_error = max(abs(datum["scipy_error"]) for datum in table_data)
my_max_abs_error    = max(abs(datum["my_error"])    for datum in table_data)
print(f"  scipy max error = abs:{scipy_max_abs_error} rel:{scipy_max_abs_error/math.pi}")
print(f"  my max error = abs:{my_max_abs_error} rel:{my_max_abs_error/math.pi}")
print(f"  max_newton_iterations_ever = {max_newton_iterations_ever}")  # 7
print(f"  scipy.__version__ = {scipy.__version__}")  # 7
print(f"==================================================")
